pulls.title: wallet: fix persistent coin lock upgrade
pulls.body:
Fix a stale persistent coin lock when a temporary coin lock is upgraded to persistent.

Previously, upgrading an existing non-persistent lock to a persistent lock used `emplace()` without updating the existing value. As a result, the in-memory lock remained non-persistent.

When the coin was later spent, `UnlockCoin()` therefore did not erase the persistent `LOCKED_UTXO` database record. After restarting the wallet, the stale lock was loaded again.

This change updates the existing lock state when the coin is already present.

Adds a functional test covering:
- temporary coin lock
- upgrade to persistent lock
- spending the locked coin
- wallet reload
- verification that the spent lock is not restored

Fixes #36304

pulls.title: mempool: remove time-based transaction expiry
pulls.body:
This is a simple mempool PR that fixes #33510.

Evicting mempool transactions by age (`-mempoolexpiry`, default two weeks) is
incentive-incompatible: it may drop transactions that could still be mined 
As discussed IRL and in #33510, this PR hence removes age-based eviction entirely.

Transactions now leave the mempool only via size limiting (`-maxmempool`),
replacement, conflicts, or inclusion in a block. The `EXPIRY` removal reason is
dropped. `-mempoolexpiry` is retained as a hidden no-op that warns when set, so
existing configurations keep starting.

Nice side effects:
- With expiry gone, the `entry_time` index has no readers. Removing it saves an
  ordered-tree node per mempool entry and drops a now unused Boost
  include.
- The `DynamicMemoryUsage()` per-entry estimate drops from three indexes to
  two, so within the same `-maxmempool` budget the mempool fits slightly more
  transactions.

pulls.title: txindex: report iterator errors from FindTx
pulls.body:
This is a follow-up to [#35728](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35728#issuecomment-6214014188). 

While reviewing that PR, I noticed that `FindTx()` could return `nullopt` even when LevelDB had encountered an error. I first confirmed that a transaction could be retrieved, then deliberately damaged part of the test’s temporary txindex database. LevelDB detected the corruption, but the same lookup returned `nullopt` instead of throwing. Restoring the original data made the lookup work again.

The candidate scan checks whether the iterator has a valid entry, but it does not check its error status. An invalid iterator can mean that the scan reached the end normally, or that it stopped because of a database error. This means a failed scan can be treated as an ordinary missing transaction.

This adds `CDBIterator::CheckStatus()` and calls it after the candidate scan, before choosing a result. Any iterator error goes through the existing `HandleError()` path and throws `dbwrapper_error`. A normal missing transaction still returns `nullopt`.

I added a reproducer on [my branch](https://github.com/musaHaruna/bitcoin/tree/txindex-iterator-error-repro). The first commit adds a test that fails before the fix. The second commit applies the fix, and the same test passes.

pulls.title: private broadcast: Extra guard against unintended non-private broadcast of private transactions
pulls.body:
Motivation: Reduce the risk of accidental privacy leak happening when broadcasting non-privately a requested transaction that had been previously broadcast privately.

Background: During the initial phase of private broadcast implementation there were unforeseen instances when a private transaction could get broadcast non-privately (see #35032 #35319 #35410 #36309 #36312 #36277 #36330).

Currently known pathways:

- Re-submission through `submitpackage`
- Wallet-rebroadcast (when a private transaction is "picked up" by the wallet, and rebrodcast after 1-2 days)

Note that these are being addressed, but other, currently non-identified pathways cannot be excluded.

Change summary: Add a general, extra safeguard: whenever there is a transaction broadcast request, check if the given transaction has been previously broadcast privately, and if so, refuse to broadcast non-privately.

Transaction relay is not affected, as it should not be affected by private broadcast.  When we receive a previously private-broadcast transaction for the first time (it's not yet in our mempool), we relay it as any other relayed transaction. Behavior is unchanged in this regard.

Notes:

- Prerequisite: This is built on top of #36477, as keeping finished private broadcasts in the queue is a prerequisite for this change to work.
- This proposed change is not an alternative to the use-case specific safeguards, but a complementary one.
- Testing currently uses the two pathways listed above. When they are closed, testing will be more difficult (i.e., it is hard to establish whether non-private broadcast is prevented by the use-case specific or the present generic guard).
- The private broadcast queue is not persisted, it doesn't survive node restarts
- Entries deleted via `abortprivatebroadcast` will be forgotten.

Keeping as Draft, because the prerequisite #36477 is pending.

pulls.title: torcontrol: send -torpassword hex-encoded to avoid escaping bugs
pulls.body:
The Tor password was sent as a `QuotedString` with only double quotes escaped; as Tor interprets backslash escapes inside it, any password containing a backslash was mangled (or left the string unterminated).

The Tor Control spec deliberately allows the token to be sent as unquoted hex "to avoid escaping issues", as the `SAFECOOKIE` response already is. This patch does the same for the password, and also adds a functional test covering backslashes and quotes.

pulls.title: descriptor, rpc, wallet: do not echo key material in error messages
pulls.body:
Some descriptor error messages quote the string the caller sent, and a descriptor can hold a private key. The error then carries the key, or part of it, into places the request may not go: an application's log, an error reporter, a screenshot shared for help.

This PR stops the quoting. A failing key is named by its position, a failing entry of `solving_data.descriptors` by its index, and a function name is quoted only where the parser accepts it. The commit message lists each changed error.

| before | after |
| --- | --- |
| `key '<key>' is not valid` | `key is not valid` |
| `Multi: key '<key>' is not valid` | `Multi: key 3: key is not valid` |
| `'wpkh(<key>)x' is not a valid descriptor function` | `Unexpected text after the closing ')' of wpkh()` |
| `'<start of a key>(<rest>' is not a valid descriptor function` | `Not a valid descriptor expression` |
| `Unable to parse descriptor '<descriptor>': Missing checksum` | `Unable to parse descriptor at index 1: Missing checksum` |
| `Could not add descriptor '<descriptor>': ...` | the same, quoting the public form of the descriptor |

pulls.title: net: parse NAT-PMP result code as 16-bit BE in PCP fallback
pulls.body:
When checking whether a gateway replied with NAT-PMP unsupported version (RFC 6887 appendix A and RFC 6886 section 3.5), `PCPRequestPortMap` mistakenly used `PCP_RESPONSE_HDR_RESULT_OFS` (3) and compared only a single byte against `NATPMP_RESULT_UNSUPP_VERSION`.

NAT-PMP result codes are 16-bit big-endian values starting at offset 2 (`NATPMP_RESPONSE_HDR_RESULT_OFS`). A 16-bit result code with low byte 1 and a non-zero high byte (such as `0x0101`) would previously be incorrectly treated as `UNSUPP_VERSION`.

This PR fixes the check to use `ReadBE16(response.data() + NATPMP_RESPONSE_HDR_RESULT_OFS)` matching the rest of `pcp.cpp` (lines 348 and 390), and uses `NATPMP_HDR_VERSION_OFS` for the version field offset. A unit test is added to `pcp_tests.cpp`.

pulls.title: refactor: move block writes and pruning into BlockManager
pulls.body:
`FlushStateToDisk()` handles block storage directly. It applies `BlockManager`'s prune locks, writes its pruned flag, checks its blocks directory space and runs the flush, index write and file deletion, while `BlockManager` reads the chainstate to pick files. A pruning API on block storage (#35627) would have to go through validation for all of it.

This moves the storage side into `BlockManager`, as described in the same issue. Validation decides which heights may be pruned and passes them as limits. `BlockManager` applies its prune locks, selects the files, flushes, writes the index and deletes the files, in the same order as before. There is no behavior change to my knowledge.

Based on #36735

Thanks to musaHaruna for his [review on my fork](https://github.com/pzafonte/bitcoin/pull/2#pullrequestreview-5533305792), which led to grouping and checking the prune limits and to moving the prune bookkeeping into `BlockManager`.

pulls.title: refactor: pass BlockManager to ChainstateManager
pulls.body:
`ChainstateManager` creates and owns its `BlockManager` which means block storage can't exist without chainstate management. Validation also reaches `BlockManager`'s members through friend declarations. In #35627, moving that ownership out of `ChainstateManager` which came up as worthwhile doing.

`ImportBlocks` gets `BlockManager::SetBlockfilesIndexed()` for the reindex flag and moves to node/chainstate, since it drives validation. `RequestPrune()` and `MarkBlockIndexDirty()` replace the friend declarations, keeping the prune check flag private. `NodeContext` and the kernel then create the `BlockManager` first, pass it to `ChainstateManager` by reference and destroy `ChainstateManager` first. Last, `ChainstateLoadOptions::prune` is removed, since every caller set it from the `BlockManager`'s prune mode.

The only behavior change to my knowledge is startup log order, because the block tree database opens before the script verification threads start.

Based on #36738

Thanks to musaHaruna for his [review on my fork](https://github.com/pzafonte/bitcoin/pull/2#pullrequestreview-5533305792), which suggested `RequestPrune()`.

pulls.title: rpc: Manual prune lock management (Take 2)
pulls.body:
This is a refreshed version of #19463, which was closed due to inactivity.

Motivation: On pruned nodes, if a wallet is not loaded while the node is running, blocks necessary for rescanning when the wallet is loaded may be pruned. This PR allows users and external wallet software to manually manage prune locks via RPC, so they can protect blocks needed for future rescans and also clean up locks that are no longer relevant (e.g. after permanently unloading a wallet from a node). This is useful both for Bitcoin Core's own wallet and for external wallets that use Bitcoin Core as a backend. Usage of temporary prune locking may also be helpful in other functional test scenarios but I didn't spend time to check where might apply.

This PR leverages the existing prune locks system we already have. The interface of the RPCs of the old PR has been slightly updated, it now matches the pattern used by `setban`/`listbanned` exactly. The locks are prefixed to distinguish them from the systems locks and prevent naming colissions. They are not persisted across restarts.

pulls.title: torcontrol: Improve connection logging
pulls.body:
Before eae193e750235e4023b3e6313284eede2cd7a022, Connect() only started the connection and returned true. If tor wasn't running the refusal was reported later and only logged under -debug=tor. Since eae193e750 (in v32), every failed reconnect attempt logs:

```
2026-11-04T14:14:08Z connect() to 127.0.0.1:9051 failed after wait: Connection refused (111)
2026-11-04T14:14:08Z [warning] tor: Error connecting to address 127.0.0.1:9051
2026-11-04T14:14:08Z [warning] tor: Initiating connection to Tor control port 127.0.0.1:9051 failed
```

On a default configured node without tor, this pollutes debug.log with 18 lines every hour.

This makes the following improvements:
- Log connection failures as warning if tor config is explicit set (`-torcontrol`, `-torpassword` or `-listenonion`), otherwise at debug level.
- Log at info level when an active onion service is lost.
- Log info at the first tor connection failure if no tor config is explicit set.

The first two commits are from @fjahr.

pulls.title: kernel: Dispatch log callbacks with btcsignals
pulls.body:
**Problem:** A kernel application whose log callback logs, or destroys a kernel object, hangs. The common way to hit this is a garbage-collected language binding: Python's garbage collector can run finalizers inside the callback, and a finalizer that destroys a chainstate manager flushes and logs (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34775#issuecomment-6278257737, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34374#discussion_r4030551866). The cause is that the kernel calls log callbacks while holding the logger's mutex, so any logging from inside a callback blocks on a mutex its own thread already holds. The problem is not new and has existed since logging callbacks were introduced in #30595.

**Solution:** This PR delivers log entries through `btcsignals::signal`, which calls callbacks without holding any lock, replacing the kernel's own callback list and custom dispatching mechanism.

The change is a usability improvement and a bugfix because with it applications no longer need to reason about deadlocks and blocking behavior from a mutex they can't see. However, they may need to be updated to deal with log callbacks that are no longer serialized and connection functions that no longer block. Compatibility details are in the commit message.

The main code change is in `src/kernel/bitcoinkernel.cpp` (+42/-77) accompanied by header docs and new test_kernel cases, which hang without the fix. There is also a commit switching `btcsignals.h` to use `StdMutex` instead of `Mutex` so it is safe to use in logging callbacks.

This is an alternative to the last commit of #34775, which fixes the same deadlock but only after limiting the process to one logging connection, and still hangs if a callback destroys the connection.

pulls.title: validation: avoid partial override of non-valid validation state
pulls.body:
ValidationState::Error() only sets the reject reason if the state is still valid. When it is called on a state that is already Invalid or Error, the mode changes but the earlier reason, result and debug message are kept. The result is a mix of the old and new error. Code review in #35570 found two places where this happens. This makes the in-and-out use of the state parameter harder to follow and to remove later.

This PR makes both cases explicit:

1. `ConnectBlock()` → `CheckBlock()` with a mutated block (`BLOCK_MUTATED`, e.g. a merkle root mismatch). This is treated as a sign of corruption and reported through `FatalError()`, but the resulting Error state kept `BLOCK_MUTATED` / `bad-txnmrklroot`. Now the Invalid state is logged and then replaced, so the Error state carries the corruption message.

2. `ActivateBestChainStep()` → `DisconnectTip()` → `FlushStateToDisk()` failure. `FlushStateToDisk()` has already reported a fatal error, and `ActivateBestChainStep()` then called `FatalError()` a second time with a less specific message. Now the existing error is logged and returned unchanged, and no second fatal error is reported.

Behavior changes:

- Case 1: the returned state has the reject reason "Corrupt block found indicating potential hardware failure.", no result and no debug message. The original reason is logged.
- Case 2: the duplicate fatal-error notification is no longer sent. The returned reject reason does not change.

The first commit adds a unit test for case 1 that captures the current behavior, and the second commit updates its expectations. Case 2 has no test, because a flush failure cannot be triggered without fault injection. The path where `DisconnectTip()` fails while the state is still valid is covered by `feature_abortnode.py` and is unchanged.

pulls.title: blockstorage: lock blocksdir in BlockManager
pulls.body:
While playing around with pruning for the kernel, I noticed that only bitcoind's init locks the blocks directory (`AppInitLockDirectories`). The kernel doesn't.

Pointing a kernel program at a running node's data directory fails, but only because LevelDB locks `blocks/index`. To avoid a second copy of the chain, the obvious workaround is to use the node's blocks directory with the program's own data directory, or in-memory databases. It starts without error, but with an empty block index `BlockManager` writes from offset 0 of the node's `blk00000.dat`, which `FlatFileSeq::Open` opens in place with `"rb+"`. The node keeps running and serves the overwritten bytes as its own blocks.

#31674 added the blocks directory lock to bitcoind and noted that "the kernel does not currently do any dir locking, but it should". This PR follows sedited's [suggestion](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31674#pullrequestreview-2560427054) to add the lock to the `BlockManager` constructor, and is based on the [`lock_blocksdir_raii`](https://github.com/sedited/bitcoin/commit/e08ecc19b37b23ee936c3b14b75b3852efd1d23c) commit.

`BlockManager` holds `.lock` for its whole lifetime through `BlocksDirLock`, its first member, so the directory is locked before `xor.dat` is touched. Creating a chainstate manager on a blocks directory locked by another process, bitcoind or a kernel user, fails.

In bitcoind, init already holds the lock, so `LockDirectory` returns success without locking again. The lock is released when the `BlockManager` is destroyed rather than at exit. That happens at shutdown, and when a GUI user retries a failed chainstate load with a reindex, after which the new `BlockManager` reacquires it. A blocks directory used through the kernel now has to be writable, as bitcoind already required.

Added a regression test to feature_filelock.py.

pulls.title: wallet: reject recipient amounts above MAX_MONEY
pulls.body:
`CreateTransaction` checks that recipient amounts aren't negative, but not that they're within `MAX_MONEY`. `CreateTransactionInternal` then sums them into `recipients_sum` (spend.cpp:1100) with no range check, and that sum can overflow.

Easiest way to hit it is `fundrawtransaction` with a raw tx that has two outputs of 2^62 sat. It can also be reached with only valid amounts through `walletcreatefundedpsbt`/`send`/`sendmany` and a few thousand 21M BTC outputs. The "Transaction too large" check only runs after coin selection, so it doesn't stop this. On master the node aborts:

```
Assertion failed: (!m_selected_inputs.empty()), function RecalculateWaste, file coinselection.cpp, line 904.
```

UBSan reports the overflow at spend.cpp:1100 first. With other values the sum wraps to a small positive number instead, and `fundrawtransaction` returns success for a tx with outputs of 46116860184 BTC each.

This checks every amount and the running sum against `MoneyRange` in the existing recipients loop of `CreateTransactionInternal`, before the amount is added to `recipients_sum`, and returns "Transaction output amount must be valid" before coin selection starts. The same check rejects negative amounts, so the separate negative check in `CreateTransaction` is removed. The new `test_outputs_above_max_money` in `wallet_fundrawtransaction.py` covers a single output above MAX_MONEY, two outputs whose sum is above it, a sum that overflows int64, and a negative output. On master the first case returns "Insufficient funds" and the overflow case crashes the node; with the fix all of them get the new error. `wallet_fundrawtransaction.py`, `wallet_send.py`, `wallet_basic.py` and `rpc_psbt.py` pass.

pulls.title: guix: produce a `-static-pie` bitcoind
pulls.body:
Use Guix to produce a `-static-pie` bitcoind using GCC `14.3.0` and glibc `2.44`. Using glibc for static builds, would be less of a leap compared to switching to musl libc (POC in #23203).

[`-static-pie`](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Link-Options.html)
> Produce a static position independent executable on targets that support it.
A static position independent executable is similar to a static executable,
but can be loaded at any address without a dynamic linker.

```bash
# file bitcoind
	ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64, version 1 (GNU/Linux), static-pie linked, for GNU/Linux 3.2.0, stripped

# ldd bitcoind
	statically linked
```

### Tested on:
- [ ] Alpine 3.24
- [ ] CentOS 9
- [ ] Debian 11
- [ ] Debian 13
- [ ] NixOS

pulls.title: refactor: Add util::Result failure types and ability to merge result values
pulls.body:
Add `util::Result` support for returning more error information and make use of it in [LoadChainstate method](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25665/commits/b1c0feb6656befc48a6840c1d841074bd6131b78) as an initial application. Followup PRs [#25722](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25722) and [#29700](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/29700) use it more broadly to return errors and warnings from wallet and kernel functions as well.

This change adds two major features to the result class:

- For better error handling, adds the ability to return a value on failure, not just a value on success. This is a key missing feature that makes the result class not useful for functions like `LoadChainstate()` which produce different errors that need to be handled differently [^1].

[^1]: Ability to return error values was actually present in the original implementation of [#25218](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25218), but unfortunately removed in later iterations. See [design notes](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/bitcoin-devwiki/wiki/util::Result-design-notes).

- For better error reporting, adds the ability to return warning messages and multiple errors, not just a single error string. This provides a way for functions to report errors and warnings in a standard way, and simplifies interfaces:

    ```diff
    -virtual std::unique_ptr<Wallet> loadWallet(const std::string& name, bilingual_str& error, std::vector<bilingual_str>& warnings) = 0;
    +virtual util::Result<std::unique_ptr<Wallet>> loadWallet(const std::string& name) = 0;
    ```

    ```diff
    -std::unique_ptr<WalletDatabase> MakeDatabase(const fs::path& path, const DatabaseOptions& options, DatabaseStatus& status, bilingual_str& error);
    +util::Result<std::unique_ptr<WalletDatabase>, DatabaseError> MakeDatabase(const fs::path& path, const DatabaseOptions& options);
   ```

This change also makes some more minor improvements:

- Smaller type size. `util::Result<int>` is 16 bytes, and `util::Result<void>` is 8 bytes. Previously both were 72 bytes.

- Broader type compatibility. Supports noncopyable and nonmovable success and error types.

### Comparison with `std::expected`

Currently, the `util::Result` class is useful for error reporting—returning translated, user-facing error strings—but not as useful for error handling, where callers need structured failure information to decide how to proceed. By contrast, `std::expected` / `util::Expected` (#34005, #34006) is good for error handling but less helpful for reporting. This PR closes the gap between the two classes.

With this PR, `std::expected` remains a good choice for lower-level functions or simple functions that fail in only a few well-defined ways. Meanwhile,

- `Result` becomes a better choice for operations that can fail in many different ways—loading a wallet, connecting a block, etc.—where callers may want complete error traces, not just low-level errors without context or high-level errors without detail. (Followup [#25722](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/25722) applies this to wallet-loading functions.) 
- `Result` can also be more useful than `expected` when merging status information from multiple calls. (Followup [#29700](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/29700) uses this to reliably propagate flush and fatal-error status from validation code that can internally trigger flushes or shutdowns.)
- `Result` may also be a better choice than `std::expected` when returning pointer values. (Followup [#26022](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/26022) adds a `ResultPtr` specialization that avoids double dereferencing.) 
- `Result` can be more efficient than `std::expected` when failures are rare but failure objects are large, since failure values are heap-allocated.

This PR effectively makes `Result` a superset of `expected`, making the representations compatible and allowing them to be used together.

pulls.title: script: clarify implicit signature-cache input requirements
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Signature-cache hashing relies on input requirements that are implicit at its public entry methods.
Inspired by the Elements rangeproof-cache vulnerability behind the recent [Liquid incident](https://blog.blockstream.com/liquid-network-security-incident-assessment) and the [subsequent cache-key fix](https://github.com/ElementsProject/elements/pull/1600), this change clarifies an easy-to-misread hashing pattern: `Write(data, size)` hashes the data bytes without encoding the size.
Bitcoin Core's cache keys already include the signature hash, public key, and signature in separate ECDSA and Schnorr domains.
Bitcoin Core's signature-cache encoding is unambiguous for inputs accepted by its current script checker: a valid ECDSA public key's prefix determines its length, while a Schnorr public key is always 32 bytes, leaving the signature as the remaining suffix.

**Fix:** Use native `HashWriter` serialization in the typed `ComputeEntry*` methods so ECDSA public keys and signature vectors include their CompactSize lengths.
Schnorr retains its fixed-size public-key encoding and raw signature span.
Return the digest by value from the public `ComputeEntry*` methods so callers explicitly initialize the cache entry, where the previous chained `Finalize(entry.begin())` obscured the output assignment.
Keep the prepared salt prefixes private and const, and copy them locally for each entry.
Retain the ECDSA salt padding and drop the Schnorr salt padding.
Add a nonce-taking constructor so tests can reproduce the encoding deterministically.
The process-local cache-entry bytes change, while script validity rules are unchanged.

pulls.body:
<!-- begin based-on -->
**This is based on #25665.** The non-base commits are:

- [`3d008913cdb` Add util::ResultPtr class](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/26022/commits/3d008913cdb697651e67cd5ee158cc12a9611c0e)
- [`2d0915656c8` Use ResultPtr<unique_ptr> instead of Result<unique_ptr>](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/26022/commits/2d0915656c80d45642965b1963f158d865846f5b)<!-- end -->

---

The `util::ResultPtr` class is a wrapper for `util::Result` providing syntax sugar to make it less awkward to use with returned pointers. Instead of needing to be deferenced twice with `**result` or `(*result)->member`, it only needs to be dereferenced once with `*result` or `result->member`. Also when it is used in a boolean context, instead of evaluating to true when there is no error and the pointer is null, it evaluates to false so it is straightforward to determine whether the result points to something.

This PR is only partial a solution to #26004 because while it makes it easier to check for null pointer values, it does not make it impossible to return a null pointer value inside a successful result. It would be possible to enforce that successful results always contain non-null pointers by using a `not_null` type (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/24423) in combination with `ResultPtr`, though.

pulls.title: wallet: Track no-longer-spendable TXOs separately
pulls.body:
In #27286, the wallet keeps track of all of its transaction outputs, even if they are already spent or are otherwise unspendable. This TXO set is iterated for balance checking and coin selection preparation, which can still be slow for wallets that have had a lot of activity. This PR aims to improve the performance of such wallets by moving UTXOs that are definitely no longer spendable to a different map in the wallet so that far fewer TXOs need to be iterated for the aforementioned functions.

Unspendable TXOs (not to be confused with Unspent TXOs) are those which have a spending transaction that has been confirmed, or are no longer valid due to reorgs. TXOs that are spent in unconfirmed transactions remain in the primary TXO set, and are filtered out of balance and coin selection as before.

pulls.title: CAT in Tapscript (BIP-347)
pulls.body:
# CAT in Tapscript

This PR provides the necessary code to enable the opcode OP\_CAT in Tapscript as specified in [BIP-347: OP\_CAT in Tapscript](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0347.mediawiki) and [BIN-2024-0001](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/binana/blob/master/2024/BIN-2024-0001.md),

**Important:** This PR *does not* include miner activation functionality. This means that merging this PR into bitcoin-core will not make OP\_CAT functional in Bitcoin.
If this PR is merged it is *not* a signal of community consensus around activating CAT nor be read as a portent about the activation process or timeline.
The PR is not a stand-in for consensus around such decisions.

This PR includes:

- An implementation of the Tapscript opcode OP\_CAT along with the flags `SCRIPT_VERIFY_OP_CAT` and `SCRIPT_VERIFY_DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT`.
- Integration and unit tests which ensure that our CAT  implementation works as expected. This includes ensuring that CAT never uses more that 520 bytes of stack memory. A full description of what these tests cover is given below.
- An improvement to `src/test/script_tests.cpp` JSON script format enabling the rapid creation of new Tapscript unit tests.

## Activation on Bitcoin-inquisition (signet)

[Bitcoin-inquisition PR 37](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/39) which contained our implementation of OP\_CAT [was merged into bitcoin-inquisition (signet) on Apr 25 2024](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/39), released as [bitcoin-inquisition release 25.2 on Apr 26 2024.](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/releases/tag/v25.2-inq) and activated in bitcoin-inquisition Apr 30 2024. The bitcoin-inquisition PR was reviewed in the PR review club [(transcript of discussion)](https://bitcoincore.reviews/bitcoin-inquisition-39). Since Apr 30 2024 there have been many OP\_CAT transactions created and spent on signet.

The code merged into bitcoin-inquisition differs from this PR, as we have removed the consensus logic which was used to activate it on signet.

## OP\_CAT Tapscript Implementation

We implement OP\_CAT as a new Tapscript op code by redefining the opcode OP\_SUCCESS126 (126 in decimal and 0x7e in hexadecimal). This is the same opcode value used by the original OP_CAT.

When evaluated, the OP\_CAT instruction:

1. Pops the top two values off the stack,
2. concatenates the popped values together in stack order,
3. and then pushes the concatenated value on the top of the stack.

OP\_CAT fails if there are fewer than two values on the stack or if a concatenated value would have a combined size greater than the maximum script element size of 520 bytes.

See [BIP 347](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0347.mediawiki) for a deeper description.

### Errors thrown

If evaluated OP\_CAT can throw the following errors:

- If at time of evaluation the stack has fewer than two elements we throw the error: `SCRIPT_ERR_INVALID_STACK_OPERATION`
- If at time of evaluation the top two stack elements have a combined size greater than `MAX_SCRIPT_ELEMENT_SIZE` (520 bytes) we throw the error: `SCRIPT_ERR_PUSH_SIZE`.

### Script verification flags

While this PR does not contain any miner signaling and activation logic and can not activate OP\_CAT, it does contain two flags which future activation logic could set to control activation of OP\_CAT.

- `SCRIPT_VERIFY_OP_CAT` IF a bitcoin node has this set to true, then it treat OP\_CAT enabled for Tapscript. That is, OP\_SUCCESS126 will be redefining to OP\_CAT in Tapscript. If this was set to true at the consensus level this would cause a soft fork.

`SCRIPT_VERIFY_DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT` When set to true, a node receiving any Tapscript transaction containing the opcode OP\_CAT or OP\_SUCCESS126 will reject the transaction throwing the error `SCRIPT_ERR_DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT` but not banning the node which relayed the transaction. This prevents nodes from relaying transactions with OP\_CAT. This  is equivalent to the behavior of `SCRIPT_ERR_DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT = true` when `SCRIPT_VERIFY_OP_CAT = false` as OP\_CAT is an OP\_SUCCESS (OP\_SUCCESS126).

This is how these two flags are intended to be used to ensure a smooth soft fork.

| Stage | `SCRIPT_VERIFY OP_CAT` | `SCRIPT_VERIFY DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT` | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1.Default** | False | True | This does not represent any change in behavior of the bitcoin-core node. |
| **2.Upgrading** | True | True | OP\_CAT is activating. |
| **3.Upgraded** | True | False | It is clear that OP\_CAT has been activated and the network has been upgraded. |

The flag `SCRIPT_ERR_DISCOURAGE_OP_CAT` provides a window of time for the network to fully activate, before nodes will relay or accept transactions containing OP\_CAT in their mem pools.

## Tests

This PR contains a suite of script tests to ensure that OP\_CAT functions as expected. In the JSON script tests (`script_tests.json`), we test:

- That if OP\_CAT is not activated that there are no changes to bitcoin consensus.
- That regardless of the activation or non-activation of OP\_CAT in Tapscript, pre-Tapscript scripts, i.e. Bitcoin scripts, have no changes in behavior.
- That OP\_CAT when evaluated throws the expected error when there are less than two elements on the stack.
- That OP\_CAT when evaluated in a variety of circumstances and edge cases, successfully concatenates elements of the stack. This includes:
  - multiple calls to OP\_CAT in a row,
  - evaluating OP\_CAT inside of a IF conditional,
  - evaluating OP\_CAT on zero size stack elements, random and large stack elements,
  - evaluating OP\_CAT on values being moved to and from the alt stack,
  - and checking that when evaluated OP\_CAT concatenates the elements in the expected order.

All of these tests are designed to cover the happy path of OP\_CAT, the various errors which OP\_CAT can throw and all the corner cases between those two outcomes.

Additionally we include three tests outside of the JSON script tests.

- `cat_simple` and `cat_empty_stack` are designed to test OP\_CAT outside of the JSON serialization regime. Ensure that we catch bugs that we might miss in the JSON script tests due to a bug introduced at the JSON serialization layer.
- `cat_dup_test` enumerates all stack element sizes from 1 to 522 bytes and then enumerates up to 10 repetitions of `OP\_DUP OP\_CAT`. It then tests if the stack element would exceed 520 bytes and if so did OP\_CAT throw the error `SCRIPT_ERR_PUSH_SIZE`. This allows us to be certain that OP\_CAT will not introduce any `OP\_DUP OP\_CAT` memory exhaustion attacks.

### Better Tapscript tests in JSON script tests

While writing these JSON script tests (`script_tests.json`) we ran into the following problem. The JSON script tests are simple and easy to write for pre-Tapscript scripts, but adding or changing a Tapscript test requires substantial work per test.
Consider the following pre-tapscript test:

```json
["'aa' 'bb'", "CAT 0x4c 0x02 0xaabb EQUAL", "P2SH,STRICTENC", "DISABLED_OPCODE", "CAT disabled"]
```

whereas a Tapscript test for the same script (annotated with comments for better readability) would look like:

```json
[
    [
        "aa",
        "bb",
        "7e4c02aabb87", // output script
        "c0d6889cb081036e0faefa3a35157ad71086b123b2b144b649798b494c300a961d", // control block
        0.00000001
    ],
    "",
    "0x51 0x20 0x15048ed3a65748549c27b671936987093cf73a4c9cb18522a74fb9553060ca99", // Tapscript output
    "P2SH,WITNESS,TAPROOT",
    "OK",
    "TAPSCRIPT CATs aa and bb together and checks if EQUAL to aabb"
]
```

Computing the Tapscript output, such as `0x51 0x20 0x15048ed3a65748549c27b671936987093cf73a4c9cb18522a74fb9553060ca99`, requires writing custom code and running it for each test. The same is true for the Tapscript control block, such as `c0d6889cb081036e0faefa3a35157ad71086b123b2b144b649798b494c300a961d`. If a test is changed or updated new outputs and control blocks must be computed. The complexity of doing this is likely the reason that no one has added any Tapscript tests to JSON script tests until this PR.

In this PR we address this issue by adding the following improvements to JSON script tests:

- Adding simple macros (`"#SCRIPT#` and `#CONTROLBLOCK#`) that allow the script test parser to automatically generate and inject a valid Tapscript output and control block to be computed automatically from the JSON script.
- Allowing Tapscript scripts to use the human readable strings like pre-script scripts by marking the location of the script in the witness stack using `#SCRIPT#`. This transforms the unreadable script `7e4c02aabb87` into `#SCRIPT# CAT 0x4c 0x02 0xaabb EQUAL`.

This results in the following JSON script test which is far easier to write and easier to read.

```json
[
    [
        "aa",
        "bb",
        "#SCRIPT# CAT",
        "#CONTROLBLOCK#",
        0.00000001
    ],
    "",
    "0x51 0x20 #TAPROOTOUTPUT#",
    "P2SH,WITNESS,TAPROOT,OP_CAT",
    "OK",
    "TAPSCRIPT Test of OP_CAT flag by calling CAT on two elements. TAPSCRIPT_OP_CAT flag is set so CAT is executed."
],
```

pulls.title: ipc: Expose Chain interface to IPC clients
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Processes connected to `bitcoin-node` over IPC (with `-ipcbind`) can use the `Mining` interface, but they can't currently use the `Chain` interface to read chain data or follow chain events. Chain data could be useful to third-party clients and Bitcoin Core's own wallet could use this as well to run in a separate process (#10102). But exposing all of `interfaces::Chain` to external clients would make its methods hard to change, since the wallet uses them as internal API (#34981).

**Solution:** Add capnp wrappers for `interfaces::Chain`, split into two interfaces backed by the same C++ class:

- `Chain`, returned by `Init.makeChain`, is stable. It follows Cap'n Proto schema evolution rules, so existing clients keep working as methods are added. It starts with the five block lookup methods: `findBlock`, `findFirstBlockWithTimeAndHeight`, `findAncestorByHeight`, `findAncestorByHash` and `findCommonAncestor`.
- `UnstableChain`, returned by `Init.makeUnstableChain`, extends `Chain` with every other method, for Bitcoin Core's internal C++ callers, such as the wallet, communicating over IPC. It can change in any way between releases. Incompatible changes renumber `makeUnstableChain`, so old clients get an error instead of calling the wrong methods.

Methods can move from `UnstableChain` to `Chain` once we're willing to support them for external use. `test/functional/interface_ipc.py` shows a Python client calling both interfaces. Like the existing IPC interfaces, these are only available to processes that can connect to the IPC socket, which already grants full node access through `Init.makeRpc`.

**Merge order:** This depends on bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess#377 and a subtree update that includes it (this PR currently carries that subtree change as its first commit), and on #36520, which fixes node crashes IPC clients could trigger with invalid `Chain` arguments.

---

This PR is part of the [process separation project](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/28722).
